video_title: John Deere CEO: Autonomous Tractors and Farming's AI Era | Podcast | In Good Company
transcript: I I have a farm myself [music] and I bail hay and the quality of the bail that I can produce is only as good as my experience set. [music] So, you know, when I think the the the hay is at a point where it can be harvested, I [music] get in the the moco, I cut it, and then I sit in the tractor and I'm bailing it. I'm listening for things. I'm looking at the computer, [music] but the end product is going to be as only as good as I am. Hi everybody. I'm Nicolola Tangan, the CEO of the Norwegian Sovereign Wealth Fund and today I'm joined by John May, the CEO of John Deere. Now when you think of John Deere, you may think of green tractors and indeed there is a green tractor standing behind John here on the screen. But the company has become one of the most advanced technology companies in farming. tractors that drive themselves, AI that tells a weed from a crop, and John is the man behind the shift. He spent almost his entire career at Deer and now he is trying to turn the maker of far machines into a real technology company. John, warm welcome. >> Thank you. It's great to be here and thanks for including me on your podcast. >> Fantastic. Now, John, you became CEO in 2019 and then very quickly after that, you launched what you call smart industrial strategy. What is that? >> Well, really what we wanted to do is get more focused on the customer itself and the jobs that our customer do. You know, in the past, what we would do is focus on building the best planter and we wanted to shift to helping our customers plant better than they ever had in the past by leveraging technology. So we realigned the customer around production systems and then really invested heavily in technology that would make our customers more productive, more profitable and and more sustainable. >> And how is it different from how dairy used to run? >> You know, in the past we we didn't focus on necessarily the biggest challenges that our customer had. So for example, when when you're planting uh your biggest expense is actually the seed, the cost of the seed. So the importance of getting seed placed exactly in the proper spot at the proper depth ensures the highest yield and helps our customers manage their costs. So we really focused on understanding what are our customers biggest pain points and what's the biggest cost to them and how can we help them reduce their costs. So you say that the goal is to help customers to do more with less. You rather help the farmer plant better than than to sell the best planter. Why why is that important? >> Yeah, let me give you an example and and I'll talk about spraying. So everywhere around the world after the crop comes up and it's it's it's standing crop, one of the biggest challenges is manning managing weeds, managing pests. And if you can't manage those weeds, they take the valuable nutrients away from the healthy plant and the healthy plant produces less. So we invested heavily in a technology that was not used in agriculture computer vision and we created using artificial intelligence the ability to see the difference between a healthy plant and a weed and only spray the weed versus spraying the entire field. that reduced herbicide application by 60%. Huge savings to our customer and they get a better outcome in the end. >> You say that you want uh more of the revenue to be recurring and and also have more subscriptions. Um it's tough to change the business model of a 190 year old company, right? >> Yeah. >> Why is it so tough? What what is a tough part of it? Well, you know, first of all, we have multiple business models that that we'll offer to our customer. And really what we saw as the opportunity to to shift and allow our customers if they want to uh to pay by the acre or pay by the application allowed us to to spread a very expensive technology across more acres. We have big large farmers that can capitalize their entire business, buy the latest and greatest technology, but we have others that can't afford that. And by coming up with a pay as you go or a SAS model, it allows us to get this tech on more acres and help more customers. >> But in the past, the farmers bought a tractor, now they have to pay a monthly fee. Are they are they willing to do this? >> Yeah. you know, and and in some cases they might just buy the the complete solution and uh and and not necessarily the tech that has the pay pay as you go. They they're very uh interested in it. We're seeing right now uh take rates double from last year on the use of the technology. really, you know, what makes the difference is if you can demonstrate to true true value, value that hits their income statement, their bottom line, they're willing to invest in the technology and and that's our strategy. We we want to make them more profitable and more productive. >> What are some of the other areas where you integrate technology and AI into machines? Uh, another great example and a very expensive cost to our growers is application of fertilizers like nitrogen as an example. In the past, we we didn't have the ability as we're planting the crop, planting corn to target the nitrogen application just to the seed because that's the only part of of the the field that needs the application. Technology in the past allowed us just to free flow nitrogen into the trench. By using computer vision, we can see exactly where that seed is and only dose the seed with nitrogen. And that allows our customers to save 2/3 of the nitrogen cost that they would have spent in the past. And and it has a sustainability impact because it's putting the fertilizer only where it needs to go. >> How difficult is it to develop this technology? I mean, how difficult is it to to tell a weed from a crop? >> Well, you know, I I tell our engineers, it can't be that hard. Let's go fast and get it to the market. But, of course, they disagree with me. Uh it's it's very difficult. You know, uh how we really got into this is we we bought a company that was focused on computer vision and uh advanced algorithm and AI, but not necessarily in the segments that we wanted to uh that where we compete. And we took that technology and applied it to agriculture. So if you think about self-driving cars and robo taxis, uh that industry was developing this technology, but we saw a use for it within our industry and really for a totally different outcome. Instead of just steering the vehicle, it's all about having precise location of the plants, precise location of where we need to put pesticides, herbicides, etc. So, existing tech apply to our industry. >> What are the implications for for like the land, the soil, the water around the farm? Well, the more we can get precise, the more we can leverage advanced sensors like artificial intelligence, like computer vision, we can reduce all of the inputs that are going into the field. And the great news is it has a sustainability impact, but the really positive news to our customer is their expense, their total expense goes down for those inputs and they're more profitable. So, it's a great win-win uh for for sustainability and for profitability for our grower. >> I believe you launched driverless tractors back in 2022 and this year fully autonomous battery electric. Pretty pretty incredible. How uh tell me how do you approach this? So again, we leverage computer vision as well as some other sensor technology and we believe it's the window for farming is so short because of weather and because of you know rain, heat, when you know when does the soil get warm. So farmers really need to move quickly and leverage every hour that they have. And we saw an opportunity to make equipment fully autonomous and allow it to do the job better than the grower can by themselves and run this equipment 24 hours a day wi without having to have an operator in the cab. So last year was the first year we launched an a commercial fully autonomous tillage solution for sale and we've had great adoption and great results as a result of it. We plan to to take that technology and roll it across every production step that our growers do because that tech stack that we developed is portable across a tractor, a combine, a sprayer. So, it's going to have it's going to lock a lot of value for our customers. >> How much of farming do you think will be autonomous in 5 years time? Well, our goal is our our our ambition period is by 2030, we want to have the corn production system, growing corn in the US fully autonomous. That's our goal. Everything from tillage, planting, spraying, and harvesting the crop, uh, without an operator engaging at all. Uh, so we believe by 2030, uh, if we can prove it out in in corn, we'll then roll it across all other crops. So, it's really exciting. It is incredible. What what's going to be the role of humans in farming then? >> You know, if you think about the the role of a farmer, they have tremendous amounts of knowledge. You know, they've been doing it for 30, 40 years. I I have a farm myself and I bail hay and the quality of the bail that I can produce is only as good as my experience set. So, you know, when I think the the the hay is at a point where it can be harvested, I get in the the moco, I cut it, and then I sit in the tractor and I'm bailing it. I'm listening for things. I'm looking at the computer, but the end product is going to be as only as good as I am. So what we want to do is we want to get the farmer out of the cab and have them work on higher value jobs, more planning, monitoring more machines, uh going to the field and and looking at the the environment that the machines are operating in and then making swall tweaks to optimize the machine. That knowledge set of the farmer is better used outside of the cab uh maybe in front of a computer and doing planning and monitoring than sitting in the cab of the vehicle. >> John, what's the coolest uh John Deere machinery you have on your farm? I would say the the coolest machine that I have is uh a planter. You know, because if you don't do that job right, if you don't get that crop spaced right at the right depth and put it in the ground at the right time, you're not you may not have a crop, but you sure won't have a high quality crop. >> And what's so cool about it when you see it when you go and kind of uh say hi to your machine? What's uh what's kind of what's the cool why is it so cool? So, five, six years ago, it used to be a machine that that used hydraulics to control the seed all the way to the trench. We've gotten rid of all the hydra hydraulics. We use electric motors. Now we can control every individual row unit independently and adjust the actual planting of the crop based on the soil fertility and put maybe in one row 30,000 seeds and the other 24,000 because of the differences the micro differences in the field. It's incredible the opportunity to shift from managing a field to managing every individual plant that's out there. and and that's how you'll get met the maximum yield and that's how we'll feed the world going forward. >> I have to say when you talk about these machines I want I want to become a farmer but uh farm income is down right and it's tough times for farmers. Why why why is that? >> Well, you know, we've had obviously a lot of disruption on on the trade side of grains. So when certain markets are no longer um actually purchasing grains uh from a country then the overall trade flows get disrupted and it it causes uh just anxiety. Now the great thing is supply and demand are pretty well matched. You know the supply for uh for crop the what what farmers produce and the demand from consumers people that are eating uh feeding families around the world are well matched. But when we get disruption in trade flows, uh it really causes uh a bit of anxiety and pause on where is my crop going to go. So this is a you know if you look at other times when farm income is down typically it's one specific country and it's related normally to a big weather event like you have a drought in Australia and all of a sudden now the we're short of crop and markets have to adjust to serve Australia. This is a global issue. We're seeing all markets right now disrupted. Whether you're talking about Australia, Argentina, uh Europe, we're seeing disruption around the world. I mean, we have markets that have come completely out of growing crops. Uh like Russia, as an example, we had operations there. Uh we we were focused on growing small grains with producers. We're no longer in that market. You have markets like the Ukraine that are disrupted right now. as well as the uh the war that we're seeing in Iran and the effect that that's having on fertilizer, the flow of fertilizer as well as fuel. So, lots of uncertainty right now that's causing that. >> You called 2026 uh the bottom of this cycle. How can you be so sure about that? >> Well, the reason we believe it's the bottom is all of the stuff that we can control, we've controlled. So, for example, what causes a slowdown in the purchase of new equipment is when you start to see overall used volumes go up, uh, or you just came off a a period where there was lots of sales and that that inventory is now trading and you need to find a second home for it. So, we've worked really hard to get our used inventories in the appropriate uh uh level that that the markets need around the world. And how we do that is we intentionally underproduce retail demand. By underproducing retail demand, uh you allow uh customers to purchase used equipment and then you get stability back in the market. We're at levels right now that we believe are what we would see at the is at the bottom of the cycle. As well as I know you mentioned commodity prices are lower, but they're actually higher than they were a year ago. So, we're starting to see markets stabilize and the overall revenue portion of our customers business become stronger. Uh, so we we believe 26 is the bottom and we'll start to see the overall industry uh start to cycle back to more of a normal uh market cycle. >> You had an issue where farmers said that you stopped them from fixing their own tractors and and and you settled this kind of right to repair uh so-called right to repair uh uh fight. How do you how do you win trust back after an episode like that? >> You know, our our philosophy has always been and and it's it's part of our values. It it's part of our purpose is to put the customer first and our intentions are to always uh serve the customer, make sure that they have access to the parts and the tools that they need uh to fix their equipment. So uh we were uh approached with uh some requests for example uh having uh our customers have the ability to diagnose their equipment on their own. We created an amazing uh artificially backed tool now that's available to the customers where they can just like a dealer technician plug into their equipment diagnose what the failure rate is. uh we'll tell them what parts you need, how you fix the machine, and and then they can make the decision on whether they don't want to fix it themselves or they want to involve a John Deere dealer or an external dealer. Uh so our intent always is to make sure that we're serving the customers in the best way and leveraging technology to do that better each year. >> Can we move on to to data? So you got a million connected machines, 15 years of data. Just how do you use that data? Well, we use it in a couple different ways. So, back in 2012, we made the decision to put a telematics gateway. Basically, think of that as a cellular connection that takes all the data, whether it's machine data or agonomic data that used to be locked on machines and send it to a cloudbased system. We call that the operation center. So now our customers, if they choose to, have all of their agronomic and their machine data in a location where they can use it to make better decisions. We've tried to facilitate an ecosystem where we allow any company to connect to that data set and if the farmer wants to share their data with say an agronomic provider that writes prescriptions, they can do that. and then that agronomic provider can create value and push it back to the customer or the machine uh to create more value for the customer. So really we saw this opportunity where all this data that used to be locked on board and was very hard for customers to use if we could put it in a safe secure location that's very accessible to our customers we could allow them to make better decisions. What's the most valuable data out of this all this incredible amount of data points? >> It's the aggronomic data. It's it's knowing what seed you planted, what type of seed, what hybrid you planted, how much rain you got during the season, when you applied fertilizers, when you applied pesticides, and then when you actually harvested the crop, which fields performed the best based on those decisions that you made. And then you can compare those decisions and next year make different choices. And in the past that was very very hard to do. Now farmers have multiple years of data at their fingertips that are that are in the cloud that we provide artificial intelligence tools for them to simply ask questions. You know, I planted this hybrid in this field. How what if I would have planted this hybrid? What would I have likely have seen as a result? So much more analytics right at the fingertips of the growers. I think that's the most exciting thing right now that's going to change agriculture. >> How do you work with the crop protection industry? I mean the buyer the sententa of the world. >> We do a couple different things with them. Uh number one they have products that they want to sell uh to to the growers. Great example would be they want to see what yield did a farmer get in a certain field. uh you know what what uh what are the soil types, what's fertility, and then if they have that data, they can write a better prescription for the next year's planting decisions. >> So we'll connect if if the customer wants to, we'll connect those those companies directly to that data. The c the the agronomic the the input provider takes that data writes a prescription and then sends it directly to the machine directly to the planter and we plan it automatically exactly how they want it planted. What hybrid goes in? What's the seed volume? What's the spacing? And we can ensure the grower that that exact prescription that was written by their seed company was exactly applied in the field. build the way it was intended to by using automation, by using autonomy, by using artificial intelligence. That wasn't possible 10 years ago. >> How different is farming now in America compared to let's say Africa, Asia, Brazil? >> So farming in America is definitely the most advanced. But when I say that, there's pockets everywhere around the world. So in the United States uh there tends to be more precision tools available to to the growers. You know Europe has the same sort of opportunity that the US has. The next uh market that that's really uh advancing at a rapid pace would be South America. But we don't stop at at these big markets. We provide lowerc cost incremental steps into precision agriculture into markets all around the world. whether you're talking India and and offering a cell phonebased uh solution that allows them to connect to their tractor through their cell phone and and monitor productivity or Africa or Asia uh we have similar tools but it's important to know that in those countries in those regions there are also very large farms that are using the most advanced technology but not across the entire countries or or continents How big is the threat from Chinese equipment? >> You know, I think Chinese equipment uh we're going to see I we had uh we've had operations in China since the mid70s. We still manufacture product there. I ran the country for three years from 2004 2007 and lived there and and ran all of our facilities. What what I think is going to happen with the Chinese in agriculture is we're going to see them focus in more on the smaller agricultural side uh maybe in production systems like hay production or highv value crops uh you know they'll eventually advance uh to larger uh production crops like corn, soybeans, cotton uh sugar uh but I think they're a ways away uh from that and from developing those technologies. We still sell our most advanced u agricultural equipment into China uh for their large state farms. But like every industry, we're watching it. We're absolutely watching it. >> Another thing which is changing is um is climate. What are farmers seeing now that they didn't see 10 years ago? >> You know, if you can look at any season um and the difference in weather patterns is is by far probably the biggest challenge. Um, you know, if you look just here where I am today, sitting in the Midwest, we have places in the Midwest that had 20 inches of rain in the last week. That didn't that hasn't happened in 10 years. Um, so the variability, I would say variability in volatility in weather, and I'm sure you see that in your markets as well, where we seem to have more extremes than we do more constant type of patterns. So that becomes a big challenge for growers to to adjust to that. You know, also as uh regions change, you see different crops going into those regions. Uh you know, we're growing corn, for example, in northern parts of the United States, and we never did that 20 years ago. A lot of that has to do with genetics, but a lot of it has to do with weather as well. When you see the impact on farms and farmers, are you surprised that there is not more focus on climate or that the focus has actually decreased over the last few years? >> You know, I I I think not I think I I know farmers care probably more than anybody for their soil, for their water because those are the critical inputs for them to grow a crop. So when we come out with technologies that allow for more precision placement of things like nitrogen, of things like herbicides, of things like pesticides, they want to invest not just because they're saving money, but because they want to be good stewards of their land. It is, you know, it's their factory. It's their factory where they make all their money. Uh so it's very important to farmers. >> Let's move on to corpor. An incredible stat. You are only the number 10 person to run a company which is 190 years old. Unbelievable. What What is it that has made that that possible? >> Well, I'll tell you. I think it's the employees that we have in our company are committed to to our customers. They're committed to our industry. And the majority of our employees are like me where, you know, they've had, you know, three decades with the company. and their whole lives have been focused on agriculture. So I think our culture and and our purpose of we want life to leap forward. We want to invest in equipment, invest in technologies that con that con constantly and consistently advance the livelihood of people's people around the world. And that purpose is passionate and I think that's why we have people uh that that have long tenure with our customer and are fully invested in our indust industries and want to see our customers succeed in advance. >> What are the part of culture that you would never change? >> I I would never change. What are you some of the kind of the funny kind of the funny ways that you do things? >> You know, I I would never change the fact that our customer is the most important person that we focus on every day. And I I'm telling you, if you walked around any one of our factories, any one of our uh uh engineering centers, and if a customer happened to be there, they would be swarmed by our people. and our people would be talking about their commitment to them, their focus on innovation, their focus on quality, their focus on integrity, how important it is to do things the right way, as well as humanity. We want to treat everybody the way we want to be treated. And I would never change that because uh if if that you have to remember as a business, you're not a business if you don't have a customer. If the customer is not ringing the cash register, then you don't exist. So you have to have this incredible passion uh to serve that customer and get better every single day. >> What are the things that you would like to change though? Yeah, I I think I we're making a a big shift right now as a company on the technology side and you know, we're going from a very mechanical engineering focused company to much more software development and that shift is difficult because you still need the strong mechanical engineers but you need this new high techch hard to recruit software engineers But you have to make sure everybody feels valued because without the hard iron, we can't deliver the software that makes the machines better. >> How do you do this? How do you get a 190y old company to run fast? >> You know, one of the things we did early on when we we did smart industrial is we delayered the company. >> We had 11 layers and we went down to seven seven layers in the company. You can't have this traditional industrial company that has so many levers levels of decisionmaking otherwise things are too slow. I mean we first company we bought was a an artificial intelligence company when I was CEO called Blue River. They had two le two layers. They had this guy that was running it the entrepreneur and they have everybody else. They move fast. So we had to make some big changes uh to accelerate our speed. What's the cleverest thing you've done since you took over as a CEO? >> You know, I think the the biggest change that that that we made that was has been successful is we moved away from a very traditional matrix organization where you had product lines and you had regions very traditional looks like automotive companies, other traditional industrials. We aligned around production systems. So, you're on the corn team, you're on the soybean team, you're on the wheat team, the cotton team, the sugar team, and all you're focused on is developing equipment and technology for a person that grows corn. That's all you do all day long. You get really deep, really close to the customer, and it's hard to compete with that org structure. And I think that's been uh the most successful change we've made as a company. >> Have you made changes which you need to reverse? you know, the the I think the big challenge that every company has is, you know, you want to be as efficient as possible. And to do that, you're always con constantly trying to determine how centralized should you be in order to leverage economies of scale versus how decentralized should you be. >> And we we have to balance that all the time. And and we're doing that every single year. functions that maybe we've put too much focus on centralization like say a supply management team that's sourcing all of our components for every industry we're in may not that may have gone too far and we need to look at that. So that's the biggest balance that we're challenged with. >> Two uh uh slightly deep uh dive questions here. The first one what is your what is your biggest personal failure in life? >> That that is a deep question. you know, I think I I would say, you know, as you're coming up through the company, um, you know, you you see a lot of things that you would do differently. And I'm speaking of now that I'm sitting in this chair and then when you get in this chair, you realize the complexity of the company and the frustration I had as an employee coming up that things were going too slow and we weren't making big enough bets. Once you get in this chair, you realize how complicated those decisions are. And I probably would have had more patience, I think, coming up through the company. uh you know I was fortunate to have some really good mentors along the way that would help me uh you know slow down and and and think more broadly. Um and then the last thing I'd say is I see the value as the CEO in having a really strong team that can collaborate on every issue. And when our management team gets in the room, there are no boundaries. There are no jurisdictions. And I think if I could have made that culture exist all the way up as I was a manager, I would have produced a better product in any job that I'm in. >> Not many not many young people are able to uh to see that. What what are the what are the part of yourself you're trying to improve now? you know, I I continue to uh you know, and you can appreciate this yourself as you come up and eventually become CEO, you've had almost all the roles in the company. And uh the hardest thing to do is to watch somebody make a decision that you know is not going to be successful. Uh and I'm I'm trying to do more of that. uh step back and maybe ask probing questions to maybe get people to think differently. Uh but it's okay to let people have a failure because you learn so much from that. So I try to ask 10 times as many questions as I do give answers and and let people learn from their own mistakes. >> What what's something about you that most people don't know? Uh most people don't know that I grew up in uh Caribou, Maine, which is a little teeny town in northern Maine where our school system shut down four weeks a year. Everybody picked potatoes. Uh my dad owned the little teeny local furniture store and you know, I had to go to school on uh federal Pell Grants because my parents couldn't pay for school. I think when you get in this role, I think people assume uh a lot of stuff was handed to you and that's not the case. Uh you know, I I I've worked for my college degrees. I've had to get jobs on my own and and really work hard and uh and I say that I should tell that more just to let people know that it is possible. I mean, you don't have to be a family a member of the John Deere family to get in this role. uh you can be a kid from rural America that uh you know came from a real small uh uh outgrowing and background and and uh if you have a passion for something you can get there. >> What do you think it has done to you as a person? >> Well, I think it's made me realize and I I tell my kids this all the time. I mean, you can do anything you want. Anything you want. Whatever you're passionate about, if you're truly truly passionate about something, you can get there. no matter how big it is or how how small it is. And uh I think everybody has that opportunity. >> What is a perfect day for you? >> Uh perfect day for me would be out with our customers uh sitting in the cab of a combine or or a a sprayer or a tractor and telling them and listening to them tell me what things I need to do better as the leader of John Deere. And I try to do that as much as I can. And I always say, "Hey, listen. You cannot hurt my feelings. So tell me everything that's on your mind that we can do better to serve you as a customer." >> How do you switch off? >> Yeah, that's that's a hard question. I I think um you know I when I'm back at home or on the weekends uh having the opportunity to maybe go visit one of my kids, they're relatively co close to where I live and just sit and talk with them about what did they do for their week and maybe convince them to go to lunch with me. Uh you know because you know how it gets it gets to the point where paying is not enough. you have to convince them that maybe this appointment is more valuable than the other appointment they have. Uh but I'd say that's the big shut off for me is spending time with family and and just hearing what's going on in their life. >> Do you cook? >> I we do cook. We do cook. Um we used to for most of my career we lived in rural America. So we didn't have access to a lot of restaurants. Uh so we cooked a lot as a family. >> And what is your specialtity? What do you what do you put on the barbecue? I love to grill burgers. And then the other cool thing I just got, my my girls bought this for me, is one of these outdoor pizza ovens, you know, that heat up to like 700° Fahrenheit with a big stone in it. I love it. >> Fantastic. I I I use mine all the time. Uh, do you read? >> I do read. I do read. And I I like >> What do you read? >> I like, first of all, if I'm on vacation, I love to read fiction. Um, you know, I also try to look for books where I can learn something. uh whether it's an artificial intelligence book or uh a book that was given to me the first uh day I became CEO that talked it's called the outsiders that talked about uh a small group of CEOs that were extremely successful that weren't known because they focused on the basic things and that's capital allocation and deploying human resources to get the greatest return uh for the customer and the shareholder. So I look for things like that. Um, I love to read newspapers and I I get kitted for this, but I still read paper newspapers every day. I just like a paper newspaper. >> Yeah. And I agree with you, the book you mentioned is is very very good. Lastly, what is your advice to young people? >> I, you know, my my advice to young people is, and one of the things that I've seen, and I'm sure you see this as well, people don't want to move as much as we had to uh coming up through our careers. um they and I understand that and can appreciate that. But what you learn from t taking on new responsibilities that are in different locations uh in the company or even different divisions in the company or even more importantly outside of the US, outside the US makes you such a better leader uh and and gives you visibility into cultures and way b the way business is done and even the customer how different they are. Uh it it just makes you a much better person and frankly it gets you to that ultimate goal that I talked about around truly valuing everybody's viewpoints. My team, I want everybody to be heard because they have a unique set of experiences that I don't have. >> John, this has been a great conversation. I'll tell you one thing, a green tractor will never be the same. >> Thank you. Thank you. And thanks for thanks for inviting me. I really appreciate it. And and uh thanks for your time. >> It's been wonderful. Thank you so much. Really hoped you liked the episode. If you did, please like it, subscribe, and put on the notification. This really helps us to get new great guests.
